full_judgment:
7. The prosecution in order to prove the charges examined as many as 9 (nine) witnesses out of 12 (twelve) cited in the police report, but the defence examined none. After closure of the prosecution evidence at the stage of examination of the accused under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (hereinafter the Code), the convict appellant could not be examined due to her fugitiveness. 

 9. The learned trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record found the accused appellant Nasima @ Nasi guilty under the provisions of serial 3(kha) of the table attached to section 19(1) of the Ain and accordingly it convicted and sentenced her by the impugned judgment and order as aforementioned and acquitted the co-accused Sabiron Nesa of the charge. 

 11. Mrs Umme Masum-un-Nesa, the learned Panel Advocate of the Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee, appearing on behalf of the appellant, at the very outset, submits that the learned trial Court was manifestly wrong in convicting and sentencing the appellant without properly weighing and sifting the evidence on record occurring failure of justice. 

 12. In support of her submission, she contends that although prosecution examined 9 witnesses in proving its case, but failed to prove the charge against the appellant beyond all reasonable doubt. She also states that the seizure-list witnesses namely PW 1 Jumman Talukder, PW 2 Dulal Farazi and PW 9 Nur Hossain were neither respectable inhabitants of the locality, nor search was conducted in their presence; all of them stated that they went to the PO after alleged recovery and during conducting search they were not present there, which indicates that the procedure, laid down in section 103 of the Code, was not complied with, though the legal requirement of law is that the search and seizure must be conducted in presence of two respectable persons of locality. In this regard she referrers the case of A Wahab @ Abdul Wahab vs State, reported in 60 DLR 34. 

 15. The learned Counsel again submits that the alleged recovery of phensedyl from the possession or control of the appellant having not been supported by legal and admissible evidence, the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence is not sustainable in law. 

 18. The learned Counsel concludes that the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence against the appellant is neither based on legal evidence, nor supported by provisions of law and, as such, the same is liable to be set-aside. With these words she solicits for allowing the appeal acquittal of the appellant. 

 19. In contrast, Mr SM Golam Mostafa Tara, learned Deputy Attorney-General, on behalf of the State respondent appearing with Ms Aleya Khandker, learned Assistant Attorney-General, opposing the appeal and the submissions made so far by the learned Counsel of the appellant submits that the trial Court was perfectly justified in passing the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence against the appellant on the basis of the cogent and reliable evidence and materials on record and also under the provisions of law and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence calls for no interference by this Court. 

 20. In support of his submission the learned Deputy Attorney-General contends that all the witnesses, including seizure-list witnesses, corroborating each other stated that the appellant herself brought out 40 bottles of phensedyl and the prosecution successfully proved that such 40 bottles of phensedyl were recovered from the exclusive possession and control of the appellant. He citing the case of Billal Miah vs State, reported in 9 MLR 429 states that although it is well established principles of law, enunciated by both the Divisions, that in the absence of local witness the evidence of police witnesses can safely be used, but in this case all the locals as well as seizure-list witnesses corroborated the evidence of the police witnesses. He also contends, as the appellant on interrogation herself brought out such phensedyl from the dwelling but of Sabiron, it proves that the appellant had full control and possession over such recovered phensedyl. 

 21. As regards alleged non-compliance of section 103 of the Code learned DAG states that a searching officer is required to follow the provisions of this section only when he conducts a search under Chapter VII of the Code. But the AM (মাদকদ্রব্য নিয়ন্ত্রণ আইন, ১৯৯০) is a special law and there are special provisions relating to search and seizure of narcotics under sections 36 and 37 of the Ain and, as such, the provisions of section 103 of the Code is not applicable regarding search and seizure in connection with offences under this special law. In support of his submission he cites the cases of Tarikul Islam vs State (6 BLC 134 = 21 BLD 140), Abdus Salam vs State BCR 2004 HCD 201, Kochi @ Jishan vs State, 1988 BLD 412, Kamruzzaman ® Babul Sikdar vs State, 47 DLR 416 and Abul Hashem Master vs State, 44 DLR 159. 

 26. We have heard the submissions of the learned Counsel on behalf of the appellant and counter-submissions of the learned DAG. Anyway, with a view to arriving at a correct decision, we are to advert to and scrutinize the relevant evidence and attending circumstances by way of juxtaposing both the prosecution and defence versions of the case. 

 29. During cross-examination he stated that house of Amir Howlader was adjacent to the vegetables market wherein he used to sell vegetables; he went to the PO on hearing hue and cry and saw two women and 40 bottles of phensedyl; he put his signature on the seizure-list at the behest of police and he knew the appellant Nasima. He denied the suggestion that on the alleged date of occurrence nothing was recovered from the dwelling but of Sabiron and he made false evidence. 

 46. These are the evidence, adduced by the prosecution, in support of the charges against the appellant and co-accused. 

 48. The informant SI Sukumar Bishwas (PW 3) in his testimony supported the FIR (Exhibit 2) story. By his evidence these facts have been revealed that on 13-8-2009 a police team under his command consisted of SI Tariqul Islam,the then ASI Md Kamal Uddin (PW6), Constables namely Md Mafizur Rahman (PW 4), Mizan Sheikh (PW 5) and Kamrul Islam on the basis of a secret information at about 12-30 pm raided the house of Amir Howlader at Misson Road, Mujgunni Uttar Para under Khalishpur PS wherein the appellant Nasima was found present and upon interrogation she brought 40 bottles of phensedyl out of a rented dwelling hut, possessed by the co-accused Sabiron Nesa, a tenant of Amir Hawlader and he seized such phensedyl under a seizure-list (Exhibit 1) in presence of the local witnesses and arrested both the women at the spot. Other members of the raiding party namely, SI Kamal Uddin (PW 6), constables Md Mafizur Rahman (PW 4) and Md Mizan Sheikh (PW 5) corroborated the whole evidence in chorus made by the informant as well as commander of the raiding party. There is no allegation that police witnesses had any animosity with the appellant before the occurrence. 

 50. It transpires from the evidence of all the prosecution witnesses including seizure witnesses that the seizure-list witnesses went to the PO immediately after the recovery of the incriminating articles and the seizure-list was prepared in their presence and provisions of section 103 of the Code could not be complied with strictly. 

 51. As regards applicability of provisions of section 103 of the Code while conducting search and seizure of any narcotics connecting offences under the Ain, we have gone through the cases cited by both the sides and also relevant laws as well. 

 52. On a plain reading of section 103 of the Code it appears that starting of the very section, "Before making a search under this Chapter...." Indicates that provisions of this section are to be followed only when search will be made under Chapter VII of the Code, wherein this section has been incorporated. The heading of this Chapter is as follows: 

 53. From this heading it appears that while the search is to be made for the purpose of recovery of documents or any other movable property or for the discovery of any person wrongfully confined, section 103 shall be applied. 

 54. On the other hand, the Ain i.e. মাদকদ্রব্য নিয়ন্ত্রণ আইন, ১৯৯০ is a special law, enacted for specific purpose with special procedure and forum and there are special provisions relating to search and seizure of narcotics under sections 36 and 37 of the Ain. Under section 42 of the Ain it has been provided that the provisions of the Code shall apply if not inconsistent with the provisions of the Ain. Thus, it appears that since the specific provisions have been incorporated regarding search and seizure in connection with the offences under this special law, the provisions of section 103 of the Code have no manner of application in this context. 

 55. In the case of A Wahab rib Abdul Wahab vs State, 60 DLR 34, cited by the learned Counsel for the appellant, in a case under the Ain (মাদকদ্রব্য নিয়ন্ত্রণ আইন, ১৯৯০) it has been observed by a Single Bench of this Division that the search and seizure are not legal as the provisions of section 103 of the Code were not strictly complied with. It appears that in the said case the special provisions regarding search and seizure as provided under sections 36 and 37 of the Ain were not placed during hearing of the appeal and, as such, no discussion was made in the judgment in this point. 

 "Admittedly the incriminating articles were recovered in a raid conducted by a police officer on the basis of a secret information. When a raiding party is constituted, then this section cannot be applied with latter. Because, if the attempt is made, then the entire mission comes out and the other party is likely to get to know it. In raid cases witnesses are generally taken from the place where the raiding party is formed. The provisions of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure apply only when search is made under chapter VII of the Code. These provisions do not apply to a case of apprehension of persons suspected to be carrying any intoxicant, or any other thing liable to confiscation under the law. The incriminating articles of the present case are, no doubt, intoxicated element and, as such, we are of opinion that the compliance of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not necessary." 

 "To obviate the above contention it may be recalled here that the requirements under section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not necessary when police seize any contraband goods from any person while in a petrol duty section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure finds place in chapter VII and when search warrant is issued under section 96 of the chapter then the require-ments under section 103 is mandatory to be complied with." (c) In the cases of Kochi @ Jishan & others vs State, 1988 BLD 412, Kamruzzaman @ Babul Sikdar vs State, 47 DLR 416 and Abul Hashem Master vs State, 44 DLR 159 allegations were brought under another special law namely the Arms Act, 1878 and in all these cases the same views were taken that the provisions of section 103 of the Code should be followed strictly only when search would be made under Chapter VII of the Code and compliance of provisions of section 103 is not mandatory regarding search and seizure under special law such as the Arms Act. 

 57. In the light of aforementioned discussions and decisions we are of the crystal clear opinion that provisions of section 103 of the Code shall strictly be applied only when search is made under Chapter VII of the Code and provisions of this section are not applicable when search and seizure are made in connection with the offences under special law like the Ain 

 58. Regarding evidential value of the testimony of police personnel to prove the search, recovery and seizure, we have gone through the cases of Habibur Rahman vs State, BCR 2005 HCD 349 and Billal Miah vs State, 9 MLR 429 cited by the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant and learned DAG on behalf of the State respondent respectively and also some other judgments of both Divisions. Considering all it appears to us that now it is well settled principle of law that although the independent and seizure-list witnesses do not support the prosecution case, conviction can be given and maintained relying upon the evidence of police witnesses, if such evidence inspires confidence in the mind of Judge or is found worthy of credit. However, in the instant case we have already found that not only the police witnesses, but also the locals as well as seizure-list witnesses supported the prosecution case. 

 59. It is to be noted that on meticulous scrutiny, some minor discrepancies are found in the testimony of the prosecution witnesses, but these are not so fatal, rather these are natural. Hence, we do not find any convincing ground to disbelieve the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. 

 "We have perused the FIR, charge-sheet, evidence on record and judgment of both the courts below and found substance in the submission of the learned Advocate-on-record. In view of the facts, circumstances and the submission made by the learned Advocate-on-record, we are inclined to alter the conviction into one under item Table 3(ka) of Section 19(1) of the মাদকদ্রব্য নিয়ন্ত্রণ আইন, ১৯৯০ and reduce to the period of sentence already under gone."
